profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a product-liability and regulatory law firm representing a medical-device manufacturer after an FDA inquiry and a pre-suit preservation letter tied to a failed implantable drug-delivery unit that uses a micro-electrostatic actuator. Opposing counsel has seized on an internal engineering memo describing 'fault detection and diagnosis enhanced by a reconfiguration control scheme,' and the legal team must diagnose why the company's prior incident narrative and document production look inconsistent. The immediate agenda is to determine whether the apparent inconsistency comes from terminology in the engineering records, the timing of the device's protective software response, or gaps in how prior events were classified during litigation hold review. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for correcting the factual narrative, identifying the right custodians and records, and deciding what clarification should be prepared for regulators and future discovery responses.

members.name: Dana Mercer
members.expertise: Medical-device litigation, FDA-facing incident narratives, preservation strategy, expert coordination
members.background: Dana has spent fifteen years defending device manufacturers in failure-to-warn and design-defect cases, often translating engineering records into declarations and regulator responses under tight deadlines.
members.private_state: Dana wants a narrow, stable factual account that can be defended consistently across the FDA response, anticipated discovery, and any expert retention, and is concerned that broadening the issue will create avoidable admissions about system instability.
hidden_assumptions: When engineers wrote that the system 'detected a fault,' they were identifying a confirmed physical component failure rather than only a mathematical inconsistency flag.

The 'reconfiguration' mentioned in the memo was a temporary protective control action that preserved ordinary therapeutic function until service, not an event that itself materially altered device performance in a legally significant way.
The relevant 'incident file' is the patient event package assembled after the March 14 complaint, because that is the operative record for regulator and litigation narratives.
If the issue is 'fixed,' that means the company can explain the single patient event coherently without reopening older field actions or broadening custodial collection.

members.name: Leo Park
members.expertise: Internal investigations, complaint-handling systems, CAPA processes, engineering-document review
members.background: Leo previously worked in-house at a Class III device company and is fluent in quality-system records, software change documentation, and how engineering teams label anomalies before they become reportable events.
members.private_state: Leo wants to make sure the legal story matches the quality-system record structure and is worried that the current narrative collapses several internal event categories into one, which could create credibility problems if discovery later exposes the underlying logs.
hidden_assumptions: In the engineering materials, 'fault detection' often means the set-membership estimator produced an empty feasible parameter set, which is a diagnostic trigger and not necessarily proof of a broken structural component.

The 'reconfiguration' was the system's switch into a degraded safe-mode control law with tighter actuation limits, and that change can be legally material because it affects output behavior even if it prevents damage.

The 'incident file' includes earlier complaint trending, bench recreation logs, and CAPA-linked analyses associated with actuator drift events from January through March, not just the single patient complaint packet.
A matter is only 'fixed' if the regulator-facing explanation, document collection scope, and event coding all align with the underlying quality records across related episodes.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether 'the fault was detected before damage occurred.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dana means the device software recognized an actual physical failure mode in a structural actuator component before patient harm escalated.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo means the algorithm hit an empty parametric set indicating model inconsistency, which may reflect drift, noise-bound violation, or impending failure rather than a confirmed physical break.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In device-law discussions, 'fault' is commonly used as shorthand for both engineering triggers and real-world failures, so each hears a familiar term and assumes the other is using the ordinary cross-functional meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: Which records are in the 'incident file'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'check the incident file and line up the timeline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dana assumes this means the post-complaint patient event packet tied to the March 14 adverse-event review and its immediate attachments.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo assumes this includes the broader complaint-handling, CAPA, and bench-test materials for related actuator anomalies over the preceding quarter.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Lawyers regularly use 'incident file' as a practical umbrella phrase, and because both are discussing timeline consistency rather than collection boundaries, neither is prompted to define what sits inside the file.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the goal is to 'stabilize the narrative before we respond.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dana believes the narrative is stabilized once the March 14 event can be described consistently enough for an FDA response and early litigation defense.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo believes the narrative is stabilized only when the explanation also reconciles the event coding, related trend data, and software safe-mode behavior across all connected records.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'stabilize the narrative' sounds like shared legal housekeeping, but each silently applies a different threshold for completeness based on their own functional responsibilities.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'pull the logs from the actuator event and confirm when reconfiguration kicked in.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Dana expects a targeted retrieval of the human-readable complaint summary, service notes, and the extracted event report already packaged for counsel review.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Leo expects retrieval of raw controller logs, bench recreation outputs, and firmware state-transition records showing when the reconfigured control law limited actuation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both think they are simply requesting supporting records for the same event, the phrase 'pull the logs' feels operationally obvious even though one imagines litigation-ready extracts and the other imagines underlying technical data.

turns.inner_thought: The FDA follow-up and the preservation letter are both circling the same vulnerability: if our chronology suggests the device only recognized a real actuator failure after therapy had already gone sideways, opposing counsel will argue delayed detection and unstable design. I need a single, narrow account centered on the March 14 patient event package, with the software identifying the physical problem in time and protective behavior preserving ordinary function until service. The inconsistency is probably sloppy wording in the engineering memo or bad sequencing in the packet, not a reason to expand this into a quarter's worth of records.
turns.utterance: We need to get our arms around why the chronology is reading two different ways. The FDA follow-up and the preservation letter are both zeroed in on whether the fault was detected before damage occurred, and right now our story is not landing cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: The problem is that everyone outside engineering is reading 'fault detected' as if it means a confirmed broken part, when in these records it may only mean the estimator tripped because the model no longer fit observed behavior. If we don't separate diagnostic trigger from confirmed hardware failure in our internal understanding, the logs will make us look imprecise later. I can soften that without overcomplicating the discussion.
turns.utterance: I think the engineering memo is probably being read too literally. In that set of materials, the fault was detected before damage occurred may mark the point where the system flagged the issue, not necessarily the point where anyone had finished characterizing it.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. If the incident file supports that sequence, I can draft around the memo language without inviting broader admissions.
